To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the rate of NEFA release from adipose tissues was not decreased when fasting penguins were about to enter the refeeding signal; and 2) the rate of primary TAG: FA cycling was decreased when penguins were in the refeeding signal.

(i) in fasting, breeding king penguins, the rate of NEFA release is increased in phase III compared with phase II; (ii) the rate of appearance of glycerol is not decreased in phase III compared to phase II; (iii) primary triacylglycrol:fatty acid cycling is reduced in phase III compared phase II; (iv) the rate of NEFAs release from adipose tissues is not reduced in phase III; (iv) in phase III
in spontaneously fasting king penguins, the refeeding signal is not associated with a reduction in NEFA release.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms that trigger the refeeding signal, which is a key event in the life cycle of king penguins.
the regulation of lipolysis, and in particular, the role of glucagon in the control of NEFA release in fasting king penguins.
the metabolic and hormonal changes occurring in the transition from phase II to phase III, and the role of the refeeding signals that stimulate the behavior of incubating penguins.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, in king penguins, the refeeding signal is not triggered by a decrease in lipolysis and NEFA release from adipose tissues.
the refeeding signal is a complex phenomenon involving several factors, and that the decrease in lipolytic activity and NEFA availability cannot be a component of that signal.
the decrease in primary TAG:FA recycling, and thus the increase in NEFA availability, may contribute to a decrease in body fat stores and to the triggering of the re-feeding signal.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the metabolic and hormonal shift that occurs at the phase II-phase-III transition in spontaneously fasting penguins does not include a reduction in NEFA availability.
the metabolic and hormonal changes associated with the phase II-phase transition in fasting king penguins do not appear to involve a decrease in NEFA availability.
, at a certain point in fasting, a metabolic and endocrine shift occurs, which is not accompanied by a reduction in NEFA release, but by a decrease in primary TAG:FA recycling.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the refeeding signal is not related to an increase in glycerol release from adipose tissues, but rather to a change in the hormonal status of the birds.
, during fasting, the metabolic fate of NEFA is not a simple function of their availability, but is dependent on the metabolic context of the animal.
the refeeding signal is not a simple signal but rather a complex signal that is triggered by a combination of metabolic and hormonal changes.
